segments.text: Music
Listening Part A. You hear a doctor talking to a patient called Mrs June Wilcox.
For questions 1 to 12, complete the notes with a word or short phrase.
You now have 30 seconds to look at the notes.
So, Mrs Wilcox, your GP referred you to me because you've been having a bit of trouble sleeping.
Why don't you tell me what's been happening?
Okay, yes, that's right.
I suppose I've always had some trouble breathing fully through my nose, especially through my left nostril,
but I feel like it's been worse in the past few years.
I used to play a lot of sport, especially netball,
but I've had to give it away because I was getting so terribly short of breath.
So while it's there during the day, the blockage, it's even worse at night.
When it's time for bed, well, sometimes the left side of my nose can feel completely stuffed up.
My husband tells me that I've been snoring as well.
It started a little over 12 months ago, I suppose.
Yes, probably 12 to 18 months.
Do you feel tired in the morning?
I do, yes.
Sometimes it can feel like I've hardly slept at all.
And the back of my throat tastes like I've smoked a pack of cigarettes.
I've tried some of those sprays, you know, those ones that you can get from the chemist,
those decongestants, just to try and help clear my nose a bit.
They used to work, but then after a while, they all stopped being effective.
Then, when I first spoke to my GP about what was happening, she prescribed a spray for me.
It's a combination corticosteroid antihistamine spray.
It was wonderful. I really thought it was going to fix it right up.
But she said I shouldn't really stay on that long term because she thought my issues were more structural.
That's why she recommended I come and see you.
Okay, great. Do you mind if I take a look?
This won't hurt, but it will allow me to confirm your GP's diagnosis.
No, no problem.
OK, thanks.
Well, it definitely looks like you have a deviated septum.
And you have some quite large turbinates as well.
Right, OK. That's what the GP said, wasn't it?
Yes, it isn't so unusual. Almost no one has a completely straight nose.
The issue is that yours is affecting your breathing, and that's making it harder for you to sleep.
Hmm, yes, that's right. Can it be fixed then?
It can, yes. The best option is usually a very simple surgical procedure called a septoplasty.
Right, I see. Surgery. I'm not so keen on that.
The only other time I had surgery was on my knee, and it wasn't very successful.
If anything, I think it actually made it worse.
Well, septoplasty is very successful and very common.
It will allow me to straighten and align the cartilage structure that exists in the midline of your nose,
and you'll find you'll be able to breathe much more freely after that.
Hmm, I just don't know if that's the way I want to go.
There are other options we can try, perhaps less structurally invasive.
I can outline some of those if you like.
Yeah, I just don't know.
I can suffer with a bit of anxiety sometimes, you see.
It's something I've had to battle with for a while now.
I suppose I'm just a little worried that if we decide to go ahead with surgery, I might have some sort of panic attack, you know, on the day itself.
I just don't know what I should do.
